I'm no expert when it comes to thermal failures within integrated packages (chips and voltage regulators). But I do know that some IC packages like voltage regulators have some form of internal thermal protection to help protect the device from overheating. I suspect the custom data chip has no internal thermal protection.

It is obvious that the Bally/Astrocade history indicates the console has a concerning heat dissipation issue.

A factory motherboard upgrade was eventually implemented, which to me is an acknowledgment by the design engineers that the custom data chip was failing due to an overheating issue. The top RF shielding over the motherboard was utilized to help dissipate heat away from the custom data chip package (see attached photo below).

When you check out the power supply area on the motherboard, you see voltage regulators, a power transistor and power resistor R1 plus the custom data chip all clustered near the front left corner of the console. All of these components are dissipating heat. Why didn't the console design engineers locate a low profile, cosmetically pleasing air vent to the left of the keypad on the console top, when the console was being designed? Instead, they chose to provide narrow vent slits along the sides of the cartridge compartment?

So, if your Astrocade begins to have graphic issues, does that mean you're custom data chip is beginning to fail (being damaged)? Possibly, but not necessarily. Some other component could be initially failing.

What you should be doing is taking some kind of action to protect your custom data chip from overheating because if that chip fails, where will you find a replacement for that failed chip? Most of the other components on the motherboard are still available for purchase.

I don't recommend attempting to pry off that flat factory aluminum heat sink on the data chip and replacing that with a 40 pin DIL finned heat sink. Attempting to pry off that flat piece of aluminum is risky. You could crack the chip's package. That's what happened to me. My first pry off attempt was successful. My second data chip pry off cracked that chip's package. Man, was I upset.

Instead of a pry off, add a second finned 40 pin DIL heat sink (preferably black in color) on top of the factory heat sink. You do NOT have to thermal glue it on. Regular heat sink compound will become tacky and the heat sink will not slide off easily.

I do recommend you run your Astrocade with the console top off to ensure heat won't build up within your console. Seeing the motherboard while playing with your Astrocade isn't visually appealing, but what good is a pretty looking console if it doesn't work.

Better yet, use a 4 inch desk/personal fan and point it at the power supply area. The fan does not need to be close to the Astrocade. All you want to do is establish a little air flow across the power supply area and custom data chip to force the heated air away from the motherboard. The custom address chip may normally just warm up. It doesn't need a heat sink.

It's so easy to set up a remote fan. You don't have to modify your Astrocade to mount a tiny fan inside it, unless you desire to run your Astrocade with the console top in place. However in that case, leaving the cartridge compartment cover off the console will allow forced air flow coming out of the compartment slits to move heated air away from your Astrocade. I've been using a 4 inch, all metal construction HOMEPOINTE fan (under $20) for years. See the attached photo below. It's not whisper quiet, nor is it annoyingly loud. My local True Value hardware store is still selling this fan. Amazon has a very similar "COMFORT ZONE" fan.

Using a 4 inch fan helps keep the heated components running cooler than normal. I tried a 3 inch fan, but it was annoyingly loud, spinning at a very high rpm.

ANOTHER COMPONENT YOU SHOULD CONSIDER PROTECTING

The Bally/Astrocade power transformer that plugs into a wall outlet is another component you should seriously consider protecting because this component is also not readily available for purchase.

I recommend installing a fuse on the primary side of this power transformer. This action may help prevent your power transformer from overheating (burning out) if there is a short or near short within one of the four Astrocade power supplies.

You can cut down a short extension cord then use 2 insulated butt connectors (or solder then use heat shrink tubing) to an in-line fuse holder there that accepts a fast acting AGC 1/2 amp (500 mA) fuse. You might be able to utilize a smaller 250mA fuse. I have personally not tried this lower value. A lower amperage is likely more protective, as long as the fuse doesn't blow when you turn on your Astrocade.

I added a brief description to a previously archived two-page New Image advertisement / catalog from about 1983.  The ad is here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/ads_and_catalogs.html#NewImageAd1983

In this small catalog, there are ten cassette tapes listed with brief descriptions of each AstroBASIC game. Each tape cost $15.95.

The included programs are: Haunted House, Quickdraw/Skunk, Guess Five/Chuck-A-Luck, Saucer Attack/Missile Defense, Sicko-Therapy I & II, Claustrophobia/Catch the Bomb, Frogway/Sloshed, Fisherman's Dream/Hi-Q (Solitaire), Nam-Cap 1-6, and two version of "Asteroid Zzzap!"

The contents of the catalog are included in this post, but are not yet online, as I'm not sure if I want to put them there, at least not in this format.

I'm using this ad to update the AstroBASIC New Image AstroBASIC program download area, which is here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/new_image/new_image.html

The catalog includes descriptions of three programs that have not yet been archived from tape.  These are those three unarchived games:

Tape #1314 - Fisherman's Dream / Hi-Q (Solitaire)
Tape #1600 - Asteroid Zzzap! (Two Versions)

If you have any of these three New Image programs, then let us know so that we can archive them.

It also argued with me that the tapes were 1200-Baud because it said that 2000-Baud is not a standard.   It has kind of good argument, as 1200-Baud is a variant of the KCS (Kansas City Standard) and I think that only AstroBASIC uses 2000-Baud tapes.

        New Image Presents
Games Available For The Astrocade Professional Arcade
        Recorded In 2000 Baud Astro Basic
**********************************************

Tape #SG1 - Haunted House
Adventure game... uses nine separate programs to play!  Different results every game.  Try to get out of the locked house by examining different items in the rooms.  One Player-Keypad

Beat the Astrocade (or another player) to the draw!!!  Ten levels of play, graphic cowboys.
Skunk... One to Four Players - Hand Controls
Don't roll a one, or you lose your turn.  Roll double ones, and you lose your total score!!!  Great family game.

Guess Five...One Player - Keypad

Chuck-A-Luck...One Player - Keypad
Las Vegas, here we come! Start with $500.00, and try to break the bank!!!

are 455 cycles of 7M per horizontal line and 133 3/4 Phi cycles per line.
Because of the extra 3/4 cycle, 0 must be resynchronized at the beginning
of each line. This is done by stalling 0 for 3 cycles of 7M. PX# is also
stalled for the same amount of time."

This has been validated. We also checked that the Z80 is still getting the
generated clock signal

"Bob Wiseman's 'Yahtzee' Fixed After 46 Years"
By Ryland Dagger (edited by Adam Trionfo)
April 29, 2026

On April 28, 2026, Ryland Dagger wrote me an email.  He fixed a bug in a Bally BASIC program that was published 46 years ago!   He gave me his permission to post his email here.  I have made slight adjustments to it to make it read more like an article.

He is continuing to work on his BASIC to cart conversions, otherwise known as BASICarts.  He just converted "Yahtzee" by Bob Wiseman, first published in ARCADIAN 2, no. 8 (Jun. 23, 1980): 74-75.  He is using the version that was improved by Rich Tietjens in ARCADIAN 2, no. 9 (Jul. 28, 1980): 82. and includes the corrections applied from ARCADIAN 2, no. 10 (Sep. 17, 1980): 88. The AstroBASIC program can be downloaded, here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_q-z/programs_q-z.html#YahtzeeAB

He found a bug in the BASIC code not addressed by the subsequent corrections.  The Full House verify code on line 590 is wrong.

590 IF C=9S=25;IF I+J<5GOTO W

The program tracks the two largest matching groups as I and J. A real Full House is 3 + 2, but the original test only checks whether the two largest groups add up to at least 5. That means a four-of-a-kind, 4 + 1, is incorrectly accepted as a Full House.  Here's the fix:

590 IF C=9S=25;IF IxJ#6GOTO W

This should address the problem because only a true Full House gives:

I = 3
J = 2
I x J = 6

He is going with this version for his multicart.  It seems like the best one to him.  He also checked out the WaveMakers version, but as far as he can tell it is not a proper Yahtzee game.  It is more of a game of just luck where the player gets only 1 roll per turn instead of 3.

As a reminder, the Bally/Midway custom address/data hi-res graphic mode normally requires a SIMULTANEOUS 4 Screen RAM bank scanning (read) scheme for the TV display.

The WoW hi-res scanning scheme is centered around four 74LS166 8 bit shift registers. These 4 chips operate off a 7Mhz clock.

The active low Shift Line (S/L) tells the 4 chips when to shift the 8 x 4 = 32 Screen RAM data out pin logic levels into the custom data chip's Serial 0 and Serial 1 inputs.

Unfortunately, a minor (?) modification IS required by you when you are going to attempt operating the Astrocade in hi-res.

1. The custom data U18 Serial 0 (pin 11) and Serial 1 (pin 12) lines are normally gnded. To remove the 2 lines from ground:
A. Cut the trace at the mthrbd bottom between pins 11 and 12.
B. Cut the trace at the top where pin 12 is gnded.

2. The 3 custom address U17 lines RAS1, RAS2 and RAS3 at pins 10, 11 and 12 respectively are floating.

I wonder how many Astrocade users are following your custom data chip prototype project with anticipation. Until I read your previous progress report, I thought you were simply thinking in terms of a data chip replacement on the Astrocade for low-res operation only. I like your bold project agenda.

# SLOT DEVICES

ctrl1                     joy

exp                       blue_ram_32k
accessory

Greetings Programs!

I wanted to share a quick update on a few repositories of disassembled code for games in the Astrocade coin-op lineup. *Note these are strictly COIN-OP versions that I am speaking of.*

All of these games build cleanly and include build scripts—you can click a button and generate working ROMs ready to run in MAME. You can find them all over at https://github.com/tinymouse42, including:

• Gorf
• Wizard of Wor
• Robby Roto
• Space Zap
• Extra Bases (Note: Extra Bases is temporarily private while I mess around with it alone for a bit!)

Things had been pretty stagnant for a while, but an excellent programmer came along and got me moving again, followed by another great contributor. Big thanks to lizard43 and MacroFPGA for their invaluable work! I'm leaving real names out to respect everyone's privacy, but I definitely encourage both of them to jump in and take a bow.

--- THE ORIGIN OF "VGER" ---

While directing AI to help write documentation for the TERSE, VGS, and VGER systems (the underlying software stack these games were written in), I stumbled into a question I couldn't find the answer to -- Was VGER an acronym or was named after V'ger (Voyager 6) from Star Trek: The Motion Picture? Since I couldn't find a definitive answer, I reached out directly to Jamie Fenton, the programmer of Gorf. Her reply settled it:

"Before we settled on the GORF concept, we talked to Paramount about doing a Star Trek themed game based on the VGER movie — and concluded there was not enough 'action' to make a game out of it. We used the name for our FORTH based game engine. The name Lou Harp comes to mind." — Jamie Fenton

Ms. Fenton even asked for links to the repos, so hopefully she stops by! I've always been a fan.

--- KLINGON SPEECH & DOCUMENTATION ---

A couple of other fun highlights inside the repositories:

1. Early Architecture Docs: In the documentation sections, you'll find "Architecture of the TERSE, VGS, and VGER Software Stack" and "VGER: A Guide to DNA's Real-Time Arcade Engine". AI drafted these under my direction; they are in a very preliminary, alpha state, but you have to start somewhere!

2. Klingon Gorf: While working on getting the foreign language speech code to assemble and run, lizard43 actually created a Klingon language version! Neither of us speaks Klingon, but online translators tell us it looks pretty good. Hearing the game speak Klingon is worth the visit alone.

Feel free to stop by, check out the code, or jump in and contribute!

That package is a 2014 Richard C. Degler reverse-engineering archive covering Blue RAM BASIC and related extended BASIC variants. That reference point allowed a number of updates to the BRB 1.1 disassembly and associated README.

* When a Degler name agrees with the BRB 1.1 ROM and every caller, that name is used.
* When two names describe the same function, the Degler/Ken Lill/AstroBASIC term is used.
* When a Degler comment is marked as uncertain or conflicts with the executing code, the ROM-proven function determines the name and description.

These are source namings, and documentation improvements.

22913:
Foreign language? (I really want to say so much here, but I am trying to
actually show what's possible, so I'll refrain)

To explain, the FujiNet carts for bus based devices have two
microcontrollers.

An ESP32S3, which runs the network stack, and is common to all FujiNets
regardless of transport,
and an RP2040 (as used in the Raspberry Pico), which communicates with the
bus.

An example implementation for the Intellivision is here:
https://github.com/FujiNetWIFI/fujinet-firmware/wiki/DIY-FujiNet-for-the-Intellivision

I will be doing documentation for an example implementation for the
Astrocade that uses the cartridge port. The issue is space. I may move it
to the expansion port.

There's a lot more going on here than would first appear, but it is done
with a pair of microcontrollers (one of which houses the WiFi adapter), and
very little support logic, so it can be done cheaply.

I just finished porting a dumb terminal called netcat, which we provide as
one of many programming examples across our platforms, attached is a video
of it running.

It's worth noting that the protocol adapters inside FujiNet's network stack
can connect to a bunch of stuff, even stuff requiring encryption like HTTPS
and SSH, so yes, you can SSH to your Linux box from your Astrocade.

-Thom

An example of a more advanced use, a Google Calendar client.

Yes, this actually communicates with Google Calendar. There is an authorize
button for Google services in the Web UI that gets the appropriate
authorization tokens, and the FujiNet keeps them refreshed. Because FujiNet
can do HTTPS, it can do OAuth requests directly, and talk to Google's
API's directly.

Google Drive, Mail, and Calendar are implemented as protocol adapters on
the FujiNet, and are available to all FujiNet targets to use.

MAME Pull Request #15906 has been accepted and merged. The fix will be included in a future MAME release.
https://github.com/mamedev/mame/pull/15906

While playing Wizard of Wor in MAME, I occasionally heard crackling during speech. In a few cases the speech stopped completely, followed by a buzz when exiting.

A repeatable example occurs in Wizard of Wor speech fragment $3C at game ROM address $9270, “Now you know the taste of my magic”. The fragment contains a V -> M phoneme transition ("of my").

I traced the problem to devices/sound/votrax.cpp. There was a sign error in votrax_sc01_device::build_injection_filter() that could make the SC-01 F2 noise-injection filter unstable for valid internal ROM states.

The calculation was:
double k1 = m_cclock * (c1b * c3 / c2t *-* c2t);

Subtracting the c2t contribution can make k1 negative, placing the bilinear-transform pole outside the unit circle. The two capacitance contributions should be added:
double k1 = m_cclock * (c1b * c3 / c2t *+* c2t);

With the incorrect subtraction, the filter becomes unstable at that transition, the output runs away, subsequent speech can become silent and the Votrax channel may buzz on exit.

The affected phoneme transitions identified during testing are:
P -> M
V -> M
V -> PA0 -> M

Because the bug was in MAME's shared Votrax SC-01 emulation, any game that reaches affected filter states can trigger the same problem.

The MiSTer Astrocade core says its WoW/Gorf SC-01 speech is a fixed-point VHDL port of MAME’s Votrax SC-01 core so it may also be affected by this sign error.

It does not really autorun.

First I used AstroBasic in MAME to export a single WAV file containing the tones of every number between 0 and 255.  Here's the basic code:
10 CLEAR
20 FOR A=0 TO 255
30 :PRINT A,1
40 NEXT A
50 PRINT "DONE"

This only needed to be done once and was much easier than trying to emulate the tone generation in python.

Next, I made a python program that finds the audio block for the selected BC value inside the exported WAV and extracts just that section. It then builds a small WAV in memory and plays it.

Then I let the following short AstroBasic program run to monitor the audio jack and set the background color accordingly:
5 CLEAR
10 :INPUT @(0)
20 BC=@(0)
30 GOTO 10

I used a mini stereo cable to connect the headphone jack on my laptop to the jack on the AstroBasic cart.  It works!  When you play a tone on the laptop, the Astrocade sets the background color to the number played.

Now I just have to write the code to control Eye-One and determine how many samples I need and the correct durations to allow the colors to stabilize and probably so error checking and of course the export code.

Commander Dave is temporarily busy with important tasks and asked that I take stewardship of his Astrocade arcade repos. We've transferred Gorf and others will follow. He'll keep a fork and will contribute when he can. The main effort will now reside at:
https://github.com/astrocadester/Gorf

As far as I know, there are 6 projects that used DNA TERSE. I've disassembled all of them and have spent time looking at the TERSE architecture and evolution.

* 

*Sea Wolf II* (1978, released) uses a small threaded kernel to organize a mostly native 8 KB game.

* 

*Gorf* (1981, released) carries a broad foundational dictionary and substantial compiled graphics, sound, speech, diagnostic, and game-service vocabulary.

* 

*The Adventures of Robby Roto!* (1981, released) joins a mature runtime to extensive original TERSE block source, showing how developers used the language and VGER task system.

* 

*Ms. Gorf* (1981–1983, unreleased prototype) documents the working cross-development pipeline: GORF4A pattern source, separate logic and graphics products, pattern and animation generation, loading, patching, and target execution.

* 

*Demons & Dragons* (1982, unreleased prototype) carries the mature Gorf-family runtime onto the bank-switched 16-color platform that became the basis of Professor Pac-Man.

* 

*Professor Pac-Man* (1983, released) carries the common execution ABI and dictionary lineage into banked program ROM, protected memory, diagnostics, and a large question database.
